claim: BACON-style discovery is generate-and-test where the generator is a short list of data-triggered heuristics (constancy, trend, product, ratio), reused recursively at every level of description. It rediscovered five or more known laws (ideal gas, Kepler 3, Coulomb, Ohm, Galileo, later Snell, momentum, Black, energy).
schema_part: O (operator library fired by data signals)
agent_test: Give the agent a small signal-to-operator table (constant -> state the law; monotone -> define a ratio or product; irrelevant -> stop varying) vs free prompting, same token cap, on freshly disguised law-finding tasks.

claim: Early program demonstrations (BACON, AM) show sufficiency of the heuristics on known cases only: variables were programmer-chosen, data were hand-prepared, noise handling minimal, and no success rates were reported.
schema_part: G (do not read rediscovery as discovery)
agent_test: Report all agent results on held-out or transformed problems, never on famous cases alone.

claim: Order of experimentation changes cost but not the final law in BACON.3 (two orderings per task); probing irrelevant variables early is cheaper.
agent_test: Add a cheap one-variable-at-a-time probe stage before hypothesis building; compare tokens to solution.

claim: Exploiting symmetry or analogy (reuse the relation found for one object to cut the search for the next) shrinks the search space.
agent_test: Ablate a reuse-prior-solution operator on batches of sibling tasks.

claim: KEKADA-type systems react to surprise by setting a new goal to explain the anomaly, unlike BACON, which only qualifies hypotheses. This is the ancestor of impasse-triggered subgoaling. Only the abstract of the primary KEKADA paper (Kulkarni and Simon 1988) was read (d17); it confirms surprise leads to explanation and says the heuristics are largely domain-general, but the heuristic list and experiment counts are still unread.
agent_test: Compare an agent that opens an explain-the-anomaly subgoal when a prediction fails vs one that just re-samples.

claim: Staging search by cost (cheap algebraic and structural modules first, brute force next, problem-splitting by symmetry or separability) makes symbolic regression far stronger than one big search.
agent_test: Order operators by token cost; compare ladder vs random order at equal budget.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: AI Feynman solves 100/100 Feynman equations vs 71 for Eureqa in its own paper, but the number depends on setup: LaSR reports AI Feynman 38/100 and PySR 59/100 under its own budget, and independent SRBench gives AI Feynman exact recovery 53% at zero noise, falling behind others once noise exceeds 0.01. Headline numbers do not transfer between benchmarks.
schema_part: G (do not trust self-reported headline numbers)
agent_test: Re-run any borrowed method under our own fixed budget and noise; report the spread across benchmarks.

claim: Exact-form recovery, numeric fit and out-of-domain error are different outcomes. High numeric accuracy can coexist with a wrong form (LaSR 46-50% Acc0.1 but 5-13% symbolic; PySR 0% symbolic outside physics).
schema_part: G3 (score by check, and check the right thing)
agent_test: Score candidates on held-out and out-of-domain points as well as fit; log form-correct vs fit-correct separately.

claim: LLMs partly recite known laws: Feynman equations give lower perplexity and sharper error drops than disguised variants. Best symbolic accuracy on disguised sets is 31.5% (Transform) and 28.1% (Synth); direct prompting without data scores 7.21%.
agent_test: Test only on transformed or fresh problems; include a no-data direct-prompt arm.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Splitting roles (LLM proposes structure, code fits constants and scores, best candidates fed back) beats LLM-only answers and classic baselines. LLM-SR used about 2.5K iterations vs 2M+, E. coli OOD NMSE about 0.0037 vs above 1. Removing the refine loop gives NMSE 1.01e-1 ID and 1.81e-1 OOD; removing skeleton+optimizer gives 3.78e-1.
agent_test: Compare: model proposes and code scores with feedback vs model answers directly, equal tokens.

claim: Even a very sparse LLM call inside a classic search helps: LaSR exact solves 72/100 vs PySR 59/100 (LLM called 1% of steps; PySR is 59+-3 in the appendix), 67-71 with Llama3-8B at 1-10% call rate. On 41 synthetic equations test R2 was 0.913 vs 0.070.
schema_part: O (spend model calls only at decision points)
agent_test: Test a scaffold that calls the model only at stuck points vs every step, same tokens.

claim: In LLM data-driven discovery benchmarks, extra reasoning scaffolds (ReAct, self-critic planning) did not beat plain code generation. Only real external feedback (oracle score) helped. Best DiscoveryBench score is 25% (biology 0%).
schema_part: G1/G2 (improve from checked output, not self-critique)
agent_test: Arm A: self-critique rounds; Arm B: same tokens on executing code and reading real output. Expect B wins.

claim: Domain-knowledge hints on archaeology tasks raised DataVoyager (GPT-4p) from 9.9% to 17.5% (about +7.6 points, subset size not stated). The paper's sentence labels the numbers the wrong way round ('from 9.9% (w/ domain knowledge) to 17.5% (w/o)'), but the verb 'jumps' and the stated purpose show 17.5% is with hints. Direction is inferred from wording, not from a table.
agent_test: Treat as a modest gain from hints on knowledge-heavy tasks; confirm with a table if one appears in a later version.

claim: On scientific-code tasks, more inference compute buys more at much higher price: ScienceAgentBench best 32.4% (34.3% with expert knowledge), 42.2% with o1-preview at over 10x cost.
agent_test: Report accuracy per token, not accuracy alone.

claim: In interactive discovery worlds agents lag humans: DiscoveryWorld best agent completes 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks; humans reach 0.66 completion and 0.55 explanatory knowledge. Brute-force solutions can score on completion yet low on knowledge.
agent_test: Score both task completion and a stated-explanation check.

claim: LLM experiment design is weak: BoxingGym finds all models struggle on information-gain experiment choice. A model plus fitted-statistics scaffold did not consistently beat plain GPT-4o and favoured overly simple (linear) forms. Explanations help novices little in complex domains.
agent_test: Measure expected information gain of the agent's chosen probes vs random probes.

claim: Evolutionary program search with automatic evaluators finds real improvements. AlphaEvolve matched best known on 75% and improved 20% of 50+ math problems, with a rank-48 4x4 complex matrix algorithm (earlier 49 over general fields); ablations show evolution, prompt context and stronger LLMs each matter. Eureka beat human rewards on 83% of 29 tasks (mean +52%) with 16 samples x 5 iterations. FunSearch primary not opened.
schema_part: G3/G5 (hard automatic evaluator; population of candidates)
agent_test: Where our tasks have a code checker, compare population-with-feedback vs single chain at equal tokens.

claim: LLM-generated research ideas look more novel before execution but not after. Novelty 5.64 vs 4.84 (p<0.05, 49 ideas per condition, 79 reviewers, 298 reviews). After 43 experts executed ideas, AI-idea scores fell 1.05 (novelty), 1.76 (excitement), 1.88 (effectiveness) vs about 0 for human ideas. Over-generation collapses to about 5% non-duplicates; LLM absolute scoring is unreliable.
schema_part: G5 (do not trust model judge; test by execution)
agent_test: Rank ideas by model judge vs by cheap execution; check which predicts final result.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-31 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Automated end-to-end science agents have documented failures: hallucinated results, 5 of 12 experiments (42%) failed on coding errors, known ideas labelled novel, median 5 citations, benchmark choice biased (first four benchmarks chosen in 82.4% of 945 runs), reviewer calibration differing by backbone. AI Scientist reviewer: 70% accuracy, AUC 0.65 (human 0.65); cost under $15 per paper.
agent_test: Add a final audit step that re-checks every reported number against logged tool output.

claim: The AI Scientist-v2 had 1 of 3 fully AI-written papers reach workshop acceptance level (6.33 of 10); the accepted paper reported a negative result. N=3 only.
agent_test: Do not use as evidence of general ability.

claim: Co-scientist Elo rises with compute, but Elo is the system's own judge. Independent evidence is limited to a few wet-lab checks and 15 curated goals.
agent_test: Treat model-judge tournaments as unvalidated unless an external check exists.

claim: Hypothesis generation then execution is bottlenecked by choosing the right hypothesis, not coding it. ARC (100 tasks, GPT-4): direct 17%, programs 23%, summarised hypotheses 30%, human-selected 33%, Icecuber (no LLM) 43%; GPT-4 had a correct hypothesis for only 49 tasks.
agent_test: Compare direct, program-only and hypothesis-then-program arms at equal tokens on fresh ARC-like items.

claim: Robot scientists run the same loop (knowledge base, abductive hypothesis, planned experiment, measured result, update) and produced validated findings (Adam: twelve genes for locally orphan yeast enzymes per the 2010 review, with the 2009 abstract saying conclusions were confirmed by manual experiments; the earlier figure of 6 is unresolved. Eve: TNP-470 vs P. vivax DHFR, IC50 0.16 uM vs over 165 uM human, about 1000-fold). King 2004 abstract: cost-aware experiment selection was competitive with humans and cut cost 3-fold and 100-fold vs cheapest and random selection. Eve 2015 shows an advantage of active screening only in an economic replay (screen a third to a half of the library). The 2009 Adam full text is unread, and the 2026 Eve study on YGR067C gave only partly significant effects.
schema_part: none (external lab check, not reachable by our agent)
agent_test: Use as design analogy only.

claim: Adding logical derivability from background theory to symbolic regression prunes candidates and recovers laws from few points (Kepler 3, time dilation, Langmuir).
agent_test: Add a check that rejects candidates contradicting stated background facts.

claim: Open challenge: integration of components and on-line revision of accepted models are weak across systems; most work is batch.
agent_test: Insert a contradicting observation mid-run; measure whether the agent revises.

claim: A weak or absent checker removes most of the generate-and-test gain. With no automatic verifier, majority vote and reward-model selection plateau after about 100 samples while coverage keeps rising (MATH, Llama-3-8B: coverage 82.9% to 98.44%, selection only 40.50% to 41.41%). With a learned process reward model, stronger search hurts easy questions because it exploits checker errors. In NewtonBench, noise as small as 0.0001 cut exact-form accuracy by 12-16% while fit error stayed flat.
schema_part: G1/G3 (do not trust a soft checker; score the form, not just the fit)
agent_test: Run the same generate-and-test loop with a strong checker, a noisy checker and a self-judge; report how much of the gain survives.

claim: An explicit hypothesis layer pays only when direct attempts are hard. GPT-4: ARC 17 (direct), 23 (programs), 30 (summarised hypotheses) at the same 64 programs; List Functions 31, 59, 69. On SyGuS, program only and hypothesis-first both score 94.3%. The limit is hypothesis quality: only 49 of 100 ARC tasks got a correct hypothesis.
agent_test: Gate the hypothesis stage on a failed first attempt and compare tokens and accuracy with always-on.

claim: With a strong checker and rich feedback, depth beats breadth at equal sample count. Eureka: 2 iterations of 16 samples beat 32 first-attempt samples; removing reward reflection cost 28.6% of the normalised score. A single small LLM was the weak baseline in ShinkaEvolve, and weighted parent sampling beat hill climbing and always-mutate-the-seed.
schema_part: O (iterate on the best candidate with detailed feedback)
agent_test: At equal total samples, compare many fresh attempts with fewer rounds of revise-the-best; keep the feedback text detailed.

claim: Off-the-shelf model judges are close to chance at predicting external outcomes. Predicting which of two AI research ideas scores higher once run: GPT-4.1 51.9%, o1 and o3 similar; a fine-tuned system 77% on published pairs, 63.6% on 33 new ideas; 25 human experts 48.9% on NLP.
schema_part: G5 (no self-judging without an external anchor)
agent_test: Rank hypotheses by self-judge and by a real check on tasks with known answers; compare agreement with truth.

claim: Active, cost-aware choice of the next experiment beat random choice in the one primary test: King 2004 reports cost reductions of 3-fold and 100-fold against cheapest-first and random selection (pairing to baseline unconfirmed, abstract only). Eve 2015 supports it only by an economic replay on a real 14,400-compound screen, where screening a third to a half of the library was cost-optimal. No hit-recovery percentage versus random was read.
schema_part: O (choose the next check by expected value per cost)
agent_test: On checks with unequal cost, compare cost-aware order, cheapest-first and random order.

claim: Online revision works when failures are exact counterexamples and does not appear from prompting alone. WorldCoder rewrites its code world model by re-prompting with the transitions it gets wrong, and adapts to a changed game by editing code (ReAct baseline 15% +-8% of Sokoban levels). In a five-round belief-updating task, most LLMs improved little after round 1 and chain-of-thought did not fix it.
schema_part: S (impasse: feed back the exact failing cases and require a revision)
agent_test: Mid-run, inject a data point that contradicts the current law; measure revision rate with and without a forced revise-on-counterexample step.

claim: Frontier-model law discovery is real but fragile. NewtonBench (324 counterfactual physics tasks, 11 LLMs): weak models under 10% overall, GPT-5 75.9%, Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4%, hardest setting 40.3% and 16.7%. A code interpreter helps models below about 40% and slightly hurts stronger ones, which settle early.
agent_test: Add a rule that requires N distinct probes before the first fit; compare with free tool use.

claim: Whether small open models keep evolutionary-search gains is mixed and unquantified. FunSearch authors say results are not too sensitive to the code LLM (about 10^6 samples, StarCoder compared in an unread supplement). AlphaEvolve says larger or mixed models help and shows a 'small base LLM only' arm that is worse, but gives no single number. ShinkaEvolve reaches a record in 150 samples with a frontier ensemble.
agent_test: Run the same evolutionary loop with a small open model and a frontier model at equal tokens on one checkable task.

claim: A fixed library of generic reasoning heuristics, chosen once per task, beats chain of thought at low cost: 39 modules, BBH +7 and +6 points over CoT and Plan-and-Solve on PaLM 2-L (+6 and +8 on GPT-4), 10-40x fewer calls than self-consistency. This is the nearest test of a heuristic table, but the modules are not data-signal triggers and no law-finding or random-choice control exists.
agent_test: Compare table-guided, random-module and free reasoning at equal tokens on disguised law tasks (NewtonBench-style).
